item.content:encoded:
Thanks for the substantive reply! That's a really interesting reading you've developed, and it definitely gives me a lot to consider. I think I'm viewing it in part through the lens of dissatisfaction with some other Foundation stories and entries where female characters are deployed only for their emotional (or sexual) value, which may be unfair of me.

I agree with the need for brevity at the end and the veer towards kitsch; hopefully the author can take away something useful.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Yeah, the twist is pretty well telegraphed, particularly in light of the color commentary in the introduction, and it's somewhat beaten in by the conclusion; I was surprised that people were surprised by it, since it wasn't really reading as a "twist" at all, just the obvious source of the narrative tension. By contrast, though, I felt that worked for the story, building the dread evenly as all the pieces came together. Twist or no, I'd agree that the ending is a bit heavy-handed, and some brevity would've been more effective there. It's not unsubtle, so I don't think the explicitness really adds anything except a slight feeling of near-kitsch. The context of the "recovered log" already lets us know that we've found trouble. Color commentary just spoils the flavor a bit.

That put aside, I think this story is actually more effective if we don't see how the players deal emotionally with the fallout, since it seems to me that a big part of the way this works is the Foundation distorting the relationships and ethics of its employees. The entire conceit of the piece is how the work of the characters destroys them, and it's presented in the form of a quotation from and by that workplace. An organizational breakdown (watch me try to get cute here) of the breakdown caused by the organization. I didn't read it as a psychological tragedy or horror; I read it as a critique of the moral and mental dislocation caused by the bureaucracy, using a very personal story as a tool for explication. I agree that reducing the female character to a token, a narrative value, is problematic, but given what's being said here I also think that's the point. The actual personality of the protagonist isn't revealed; rather, it's reduced by structure to fit the needs of a Foundation report, narrowed to a case-sensitive summary for the benefit of study. The character of Christina is effaced twice, once by her husband, and once again by the Foundation when it strips her to an artifact to understand that husband's madness. The former perspective is implicitly and explicitly tainted, in itself, by the latter. To illustrate the extremity of that, and as a cute little touch, check out the timestamps: The Foundations kept this guy actively working for another ~10 years, and never even told him that Christina killed herself.

It looks sort of like a basic "man's inhumanity to man" thing, but the absence of an antagonist means that it becomes, so to speak, nobody's fault, and thus ruminates instead on the catalyst (and presenter) of the story, the bureaucracy. It's an inhuman structure made by humans, and it ultimately reflects its own inhuman values onto its creators. That's actually another point of criticism for me: Given the context and import of the frame story, it would work much better to drop the color commentary on Dr. ██████'s psychological background and condition, as well as lose the (un)named analysts, since that attaches both an opinion and a face (however inscrutable and vague) to the Foundation. It undermines the theme a bit, at least to me.

Anyways, I'm getting afield here. Nice, meaty critique there, battuta, I (clearly) think there should be more of that around here. Welcome.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Interesting piece. I think the twist is a little too obvious from about the halfway point on - 'she's pregnant' pops up instantly the moment she starts behaving oddly, since it's such a familiar trope of relationship stories. From there, the ending feels obvious too; 'he kills the baby' has that ironic weight to it. That's not always a bad thing, since the trepidation of a foreseen but seemingly unavoidable catastrophe is part of what makes a tragedy compelling, but in this case it detracted from the narrative for me, and not just because the ending spells out what's already pretty obvious.

I've gone back and forth a bit on whether the story felt contrived to me. Foundation researchers would, obviously, be watched carefully, but this type of psychological disintegration sneaks up on everyone, and in reality we've seen plenty of monsters born from that nice guy next door. And while the wife character was clearly intelligent, I can buy that she didn't see this coming…even if that blindness, and her subsequent suicide, plays into a long and slightly queasy SCP tradition of using women as shortcuts to an easy emotional response. Here, too, I quibbled over possible criticism - an intelligent woman doing meaningful work has a lot more to live for than a child - but losing both a husband and an unborn child is a serious blow, and I can buy that it could drive anyone to suicide, even if it's a touch cliche. It might be more devastating to see her live with the consequences than to play to the familiar 'my child is everything!' story.

I think that's perhaps what nags at me - the story reads like it's trying a bit too hard at the end. An abortion, a suicide, madness, eventual termination: it's all very feel bad, feel bad, in a cheap way that short-circuits any really tragic examination of the consequences. People living with a tragedy can be a lot more difficult than people doing themselves in, and it would reinforce the idea that Christina is a real person, rather than a cheap token in a story mostly concerned with the inner life of a slightly dim main character.

I think I'll downvote for now, but your prose is quite solid and you're clearly a capable storyteller.
